/-!
# Hypothesis H

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schinzel%27s_hypothesis_H)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Polynomial
namespace Schinzel

/--
**Schinzel conjecture (H hypothesis)**
If a finite set of polynomials $f_i$ satisfies both Schinzel and Bunyakovsky conditions,
there exist infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that $f_i(n)$ are primes for all $i$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem schinzel_conjecture (fs : Finset ℤ[X]) (hfs : ∀ f ∈ fs, BunyakovskyCondition f)
    (hfs' : SchinzelCondition fs) : Infinite {n : ℕ | ∀ f ∈ fs, (f.eval (n : ℤ)).natAbs.Prime} := by
  sorry

end Schinzel

reformulations.difference: Lean assumes the absence of a fixed prime obstruction and asserts infinitude of natural inputs for which all absolute values are prime. Wikipedia instead states a dichotomy: infinitely many positive inputs with simultaneous positive prime values, or a fixed divisor greater than 1 of the product.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: BunyakovskyCondition supplies exactly the stated nonconstancy, irreducibility, and positive leading coefficients. A prime divides a finite product iff it divides a factor, and every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor, so SchinzelCondition negates the fixed-divisor alternative. A local witness n can be replaced by n+p to make it positive without changing divisibility modulo p. Each permitted polynomial is positive for all sufficiently large natural inputs; finiteness of the family gives a common threshold. Thus taking absolute values and including n=0 change only finitely many candidate inputs, not infinitude. The full equivalence with the positive-input dichotomy was proved as wikipedia_equivalence in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
